**Conversation Overview**

This conversation is a long-running technical book production session for a project called "The Method 1.6," a publishable multi-volume series of books covering an original mathematical/physical framework involving configuration-space lattices, spectral data, and related theoretical structures. The person is the author and project owner, overseeing the build of six volumes: a main volume, a Register, and four compendia (Mathematical, Physics, Index of Indices, and Spectra). The work is managed through a highly structured protocol involving numbered rulings, working-register entries (W-entries), build bundles (BUILD-52/53), session handoffs (HANDOFF-52/53), and a mandatory reading gate that must be executed at the start of each session to verify build identity from file measurements rather than memory.

The session accomplished several major items. A long-standing blocker (ledger item 7) was resolved: the coordinates gate in the build instrument was mis-firing on the Register because Register entries quoting Spectra's build-time claim triggered the file-wide check, causing the Register press to abort. The author issued Ruling 65 scoping the coords tool to the Spectra volume only, identified by its H1 title marker. This was implemented, verified across all six volumes, and the Register was successfully pressed and delivered as the sixth volume (396 pages, 394 folios) for the first time since chat 24. A producer bug in index_pages.py (W-082) was repaired by narrowing the drift-slack to zero for numeral-terminated headings, preventing prose lines from stealing page mappings. A sound Contents checker was built per §3a.1 specifications, and all six previously flagged candidate Contents mis-pages were established as artifacts of the prior unsound checker — zero real mis-pages exist. Math, Physics, and Spectra compendia were re-pressed and verified. BUILD-53 was packed as 120 members with full round-trip verification.

A significant provenance question was investigated: why the Register begins at entry 165 rather than 1. Research into earlier Drive materials (The Method 1.2 and the Lach Elemental Lattice paper) established that the Register has always started at 165, and entries 1–94 belong to the three-coordinate (n, ℓ, k) elemental lattice (the first paper), while entries ~95–164 correspond to the successor eight-coordinate Λ₈/Lach Cylinder object whose text is unretrievable. The author engaged with the Lach Elemental Lattice project to obtain a genesis register block, which returned K=94 entries. These were verified against the Drive paper with every load-bearing number confirmed exact. Ruling 66 was issued settling the seating plan: seat all 94 entries flat in chronological order without part headers, with entries 95–164 each individually marked as superseded and pointed to their own distinct superseding entry found by reading the entire register — this mapping task is deferred to chat 52. BUILD-53 and HANDOFF-53 were rebuilt to carry Ruling 66 and W-089 (the seating task specification) before the session closed.

**Tool Knowledge**

Google Drive file downloads using the `download_file_content` tool with large files (the figures archive at ~6.3 MB) spill to disk at `/mnt/user-data/tool_results/[tool_call_id].json` rather than returning inline, requiring a Python decode step using `json.load` followed by base64 decode with `validate=True` and md5 verification before use. The authoritative verification is the md5 hash, not the byte count. The figures archive Drive file ID is `1q7pvnxMPILD9AVoH6XjymZHXX79YzITd` (6,299,293 bytes, md5 `78888f2078dc5342ab221a59bbcf8921`), unpacking to `figures/` (49 files) and `figures-compendia/` (12 files). The Lach Elemental Lattice paper Drive file ID is `1KYAiKSItbYHW9Dk3Cg1txWSrDD4cTJaB`. Broad Drive searches using `fullText contains` or `title contains` on general terms may surface unrelated personal files in the same Drive; these should be disregarded without reference. The project enforces that all file measurements must be taken from split build files, never

# keeping it re-admits the Contents. Every Contents entry carries leader dots and no real heading
# does, so the dots are the discriminator. front stays only to drop a title page when one exists.
def bodylines(p): return [l for l in p.splitlines() if '……' not in l]
front=0
pm={}
for loc,h in heads.items():
    num=loc.replace('§','').replace('App ','appendix '); want=norm(num+' '+h) if not loc.startswith('H:') else norm(h)
    for i,p in enumerate(pages):
        if i<front: continue
        lines=[norm(l) for l in bodylines(p)]
        # W-082 (chat 50). The prefix branch below carries six characters of slack for PDF text drift.
        # For a heading whose ONLY discriminator is a trailing numeral the slack deletes exactly the
        # discriminator, and a PROSE line that merely opens with the same words then takes the mapping
        # — Physics 'channel equation, a — 0.3772' was captured by p14's 'channel equation a 8 channel
        # equation e0 8 ...' four pages ahead of its own heading. The slack is KEPT, because drift
        # truncates a heading; the guard is that a heading line cannot be much LONGER than the heading.

This is W-013's design and it is the good kind of gate — it catches a claim that is true of the printed result but false of the mechanism, the drift nothing else would catch.

**Why it now fires on the Register.** `coords.py` is a *Spectra* instrument — its own header declares `usage: coords.py <spectra.md>`, and it knows how to reconcile Spectra's Part 0 figure table against the companion. When the gate was written it fired on Spectra alone, and the Register pressed cleanly to 388 pp at chat 24. Since then, Register entries appended in the normal course of the work **quote** the Spectra Compendium's build-time reading — L5891 literally reads *"read from the data companion at build."* The gate's trigger is file-wide, so it can't tell *"this volume makes the claim about itself"* from *"this volume quotes another volume's claim as subject matter."* It fires, runs `coords.py` on the Register, `coords.py` finds no Part 0 table there, returns exit 1 (ten sites not found), and the press aborts. So the Register — the sixth volume — is the only one not delivered. This is a regression from legitimate, append-only growth, not from an edit or a content defect.

**What will not work (so you don't spend a ruling on it).** Two narrowings were designed and both died on measurement: (1) *require the companion's name inside the matching phrase* — dead, because Spectra's own claims ("read from it at build," "read from the coordinate companion at build") don't name the file inline, so this would silently disarm the gate on the one volume it exists for; (2) *require the structural section `coords.py` reads* — dead, because `coords.py` deliberately exits loud on a missing section, so this would turn a loud failure into a silent skip. Both fail the same way: they make the gate pass quietly when it should fire. Editing the Register to remove the quotes is also off the table — it's append-only and the quotes are legitimate subject matter; rewriting them at press to dodge a gate is precisely the "change prose to make a discrepancy disappear" the project forbids.

**The one coherent repair — and the single thing you need to rule.** `coords.py` is to Spectra exactly what `appf.py` is to the main volume, and `appf` is already gated to run *main-only*, identified by content (`# PART 0`), not by filename. The same class of repair applies here: **scope the coords gate to run only on the Spectra volume**, identified by a Spectra-specific marker the Register does not contain. That is a repair to an existing mechanism, the same authorized class as `appf`'s content-gate — it needs your ruling only because it changes *what a gate guards*, and because the identifying marker must be chosen so it can't itself be silently disarmed by a later rename (the trap that killed narrowing 2).

# Print index: map every §-locator in the main volume's Index block to the page its heading
# starts on in a pressed PDF, and write a press-only copy of the source with page numbers in the Index.
# usage: python3 index_pages.py <src.md> <first-pass.pdf> <out.md>
import re,sys,subprocess
src,pdf,out=sys.argv[1:4]
L=open(src,encoding='utf-8').read().splitlines()
heads={}   # locator -> heading text
allh=[]    # (level, text) for the generic Contents
DEPTH=int(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv)>4 else 2
body=[i for i,l in enumerate(L) if l.startswith('# PART 0')]
body=body[-1] if body else 1
for l in L[body:]:
    mh=re.match(r'^(#{1,3}) (.*)',l)
    if mh and len(mh.group(1))<=DEPTH+1 and not l.startswith('# PART'): allh.append((len(mh.group(1)),mh.group(2))); heads.setdefault('H:'+mh.group(2),mh.group(2))
    m=re.match(r'^## (\d+)\. (.*)',l)
    if m: heads.setdefault('§'+m.group(1),m.group(2)); continue
    m=re.match(r'^### (\d+\.\d+) (.*)',l)
    if m: heads.setdefault('§'+m.group(1),m.group(2)); continue
    m=re.match(r'^## Appendix ([A-Z]) — (.*)',l)
    if m: heads.setdefault('App '+m.group(1),m.group(2))
pages=subprocess.run(['pdftotext','-layout',pdf,'-'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.split('\f')
def norm(s): return re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9]+',' ',re.sub(r'\*|_|`','',s).lower()).strip()
ptext=[norm(p) for p in pages]
# the printed TOC also carries every heading: take the LAST page after the front matter on which the heading opens a line
haslit=any(re.match(r'^\s*#{0,3}\s*Contents\s*$',l) for l in L)
# FRONT BOUNDARY BY CONTENT (chat 16). The old rule was positional — `i>3` for a literal Contents,
# `1` otherwise — and both let a heading match ITSELF inside the printed Contents. That produced a
# STABLE WRONG map: once an entry read page N, the Contents on page N kept re-matching it there, and
# the convergence check passed. Measured at BUILD-16: math ~139/308, ioi 29/61, physics 24/61,
# spectra 5/31, main 13 entries plus every App locator. Convergence is not correctness.
# A Contents page is identified by its leader dots, not by its number.
# The boundary is a LINE, not a page. A page-level skip cannot work: in the Index of Indices the
# Contents tail and the first body heading share page 2, so skipping the page loses the heading and
# keeping it re-admits the Contents. Every Contents entry carries leader dots and no real heading
# does, so the dots are the discriminator. front stays only to drop a title page when one exists.
def bodylines(p): return [l for l in p.splitlines() if '……' not in l]
front=0
pm={}
for loc,h in heads.items():
    num=loc.replace('§','').replace('App ','appendix '); want=norm(num+' '+h) if not loc.startswith('H:') else norm(h)
    for i,p in enumerate(pages):
        if i<front: continue
        lines=[norm(l) for l in bodylines(p)]
        # W-082 (chat 50). The prefix branch below carries six characters of slack for PDF text drift.
        # For a heading whose ONLY discriminator is a trailing numeral the slack deletes exactly the
        # discriminator, and a PROSE line that merely opens with the same words then takes the mapping
        # — Physics 'channel equation, a — 0.3772' was captured by p14's 'channel equation a 8 channel
        # equation e0 8 ...' four pages ahead of its own heading. The slack is KEPT, because drift
        # truncates a heading; the guard is that a heading line cannot be much LONGER than the heading.
        if any(l==want or (len(want)>12 and l.startswith(want[:max(12,len(want)-6)]) and len(l)<=len(want)+6) or (l.startswith(norm(num)+' ') and want.startswith(l) and len(l)>len(norm(num))+8) for l in lines):
            pm[loc]=i+1; break
    # WRAPPED-HEADING FALLBACK (chat 16). The test above compares whole LINES, so a heading long
    # enough to wrap in the PDF matches nothing and drops out of the Contents silently. norm() over
    # the whole page collapses the wrap. Long headings only, so a short string cannot match spuriously.
    if loc not in pm and len(want)>18:
        for i,p in enumerate(pages):
            if i<front: continue
            if want in norm("\n".join(bodylines(p))): pm[loc]=i+1; break
print('headings',len(heads),'mapped',len(pm))
_un=[k for k in heads if k not in pm]
if _un: print('UNMAPPED HEADINGS (absent from the Contents):',[ (k, heads[k][:60]) for k in _un ])
ixs=[i for i,l in enumerate(L) if l.startswith('## Index')]
ix=ixs[-1] if ixs else len(L)
missing=set(); n=0
def sub(m):
    global n
    loc=m.group(0); n+=1
    if loc in pm: return f'{loc} ({pm[loc]})'
    missing.add(loc); return loc
for i in range(ix,len(L)):
    if L[i].startswith('## ') and i>ix: break
    if '……' in L[i]: L[i]=re.sub(r'§\d+(?:\.\d+)?|App [A-Z]',sub,L[i])
print('locators',n,'unmapped',sorted(missing)[:20],len(missing))
# Contents with page numbers, replacing the source's literal contents block (which build.py otherwise strips)
ci=[i for i,l in enumerate(L) if re.match(r'^\s*#{0,3}\s*Contents\s*$',l)]
if ci:
    i=ci[0]; parts=[k for k,l in enumerate(L) if k>i and re.match(r'^# PART 0',l)]; j=parts[1] if len(parts)>1 else i+1
    toc=['## Contents','']
    for l in L[body:]:
        m=re.match(r'^# (PART .*)',l)
        if m:
            if m.group(1).startswith('PART 0'): continue   # RULED, author, chat 16: PART 0 is not listed
            toc.append(''); toc.append('**'+m.group(1)+'**'); toc.append(''); continue
        m=re.match(r'^## (\d+)\. (.*)',l)
        # `1. ` at line start is an ORDERED LIST to pandoc, so every chapter printed as a list item
        # with list spacing (chat 16, found in the object). Escaping the period keeps it a plain line.
        if m: toc.append(f"{m.group(1)}\\. {m.group(2)} …… {pm.get('§'+m.group(1),'')}  "); continue
        m=re.match(r'^## (Appendix [A-Z]) — (.*)',l)
        if m: toc.append(f"{m.group(1)} — {m.group(2)} …… {pm.get('App '+m.group(1)[-1],'')}  "); continue
        m=re.match(r'^## (Index|References)\b',l)
        if m: toc.append(f"{m.group(1)}  "); continue
    L=L[:i]+toc+['']+L[j:]
    print('contents block written',len(toc),'lines')
else:
    _title=allh[0][1] if allh and allh[0][0]==1 else None   # a volume's own title is not a Contents entry
    toc=['## Contents','']+[('  ' if lv==3 else '')+f"{h} …… {pm.get('H:'+h,'')}  " for lv,h in allh if h!='Contents' and h!=_title and pm.get('H:'+h)]
    k=1 if L and L[0].startswith('# ') else 0
    L=L[:k]+['']+toc+['']+L[k:]
    print('generic contents written',len(toc)-2,'headings')
open(out,'w',encoding='utf-8').write('\n'.join(L)+'\n')

# THE METHOD 1.6 — THE REGISTER

## Why this register is printed

**1465 entries, 165 to 1786.** Each is written at a fixed density and stands alone. *The register is the working record the five compendia are distilled from. It is printed because a result is worth what its derivation is worth: the measurements as they were taken, the arguments as they were made, and the reversals kept beside the claims they overturned. The compendia answer; this is where the answers were got — including the ones that were got wrong first.*

**A correction never replaces what it corrects.** Both states are kept, and the entry that corrects names the entry corrected, so the record of a mistake survives its repair. It is the discipline the volume rests on: a register that tidied itself would be evidence of nothing.

**Every entry has one form: a capitalised headline, then the body in italics** (entry 1725 records how the form was reached).

**An entry is cited by a chapter, by a compendium object, or by another entry. Nothing here is decorative — an entry exists because something rests on it.**

### The order the entries are in

Entries run in the order the work happened, which is why they are numbered rather than arranged. **Thirty-two of the earliest fault entries (203–354) are the one exception:** they are printed together after entry 361, under headings that list every number they hold, because what those entries share is a mechanism rather than a moment.

### What the entries are

| kind | entries (Build 16) | first reading | what it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a finding** | 1,268 | 796 | something established that was not known before the entry |
| **a correction** | 140 | 370 | something written wrong and put right, with both states kept |
| **a measurement** | 476 | 299 | a number, with what it was measured on |
| **prior art** | 53 | 69 | a result found to be published, with the source |
| **a new protocol** | 62 | 67 | a rule earned by a failure, so the failure cannot recur |
| **a withdrawal** | 29 | 61 | a claim removed, with the reason |
| **a fault of mine** | 16 | 59 | an error by the assistant, recorded as such |
| **an open question** | 23 | 30 | something the work cannot currently settle, and why |

*The kinds overlap: a correction is usually also a measurement, and a withdrawal usually cites prior art. The counts are of entries matching each pattern, not a partition.* *The Build 16 column is recomputed from this file by `kinds.py` over the 1,465 entry headings, seven of which hold the thirty-two grouped fault entries: an entry is counted under a kind when its headline matches that kind's pattern — a correction on CORRECT, WRONG, STALE, PUT RIGHT, AMEND, FIX, MISLOCATED, REPAIR, ERROR, OVERTAKEN, MISTAKEN, MISREAD, MISCOUNTED; a measurement when the headline carries a number; prior art on PRIOR ART, PUBLISHED, ALREADY KNOWN or a year; a new protocol on PROTOCOL, RULE, RULED, RULING, MUST, PROCEDURE; a withdrawal on WITHDRAWN, RETRACTED, REMOVED, DROPPED, ABANDONED, DISCARDED; a fault of mine on FAULT OF MINE, MY FAULT, MY ERROR, THE ASSISTANT; an open question on OPEN QUESTION, OPEN, UNSETTLED, UNRESOLVED, UNKNOWN, NOT YET KNOWN; a finding otherwise, unless it is a correction, withdrawal, fault or open question; a body tag such as "(a measurement.)" overrides the pattern; the ten grouped headings count as corrections and faults. The first-reading column ( and earlier) was produced by patterns that were never printed and is kept as the reading it was.*

### The load-bearing entries

**571 entries are cited by other entries.** *A citation is counted each time an entry names another — "register 1460", "R 1460", or a range — so an entry cited three times by one entry counts three; an entry does not count as citing itself. Recomputed from this file by `register_cites.py` (2026-08-26).* Those cited most are the ones the rest of the record leans on — the 11 cited seven times or more:

| entry | cited | what it established |
|---|---|---|
| **1460** | 10× | ν is deactivated as a law and retained as a form; the corridor is the instrument and it survives intact |
| **1475** | 10× | Maximality is bracketed by observability, and the register already defined the bracket |
| **784** | 9× | The fault was invisible to every audit because the audits check consistency, not provenance |
| **1581** | 9× | Six candidate axes tested: five are determined, Z is refused at 2.1%, and H1's re-coordinatisation does not close |
| **1649** | 9× | Incorporation phase 3 — the charge-0 face computed: 554 series cells staged |
| **1664** | 9× | 145 of 554 carry a δ computed against the wrong core — and R 1649's fallback is the silent default §2.9 forbids |
| **1578** | 9× | IMPROBABLE is removed from the index altogether — it was a judgement about the future standing in a column of facts |
| **1020** | 8× | A proposal was made that Θ = 0 might supply the missing relative boost; it fails, and the reason is clean |
| **1445** | 8× | The 99 was fitted, not generated: held out the walk scores 90 and plain Madelung beats it |
| **1462** | 7× | And the ratio-4 identity is not a step toward the proof — it is the proof, because it makes the constraint matrix rank one |
| **1595** | 7× | I was wrong that the ladder needs a URL from M — he supplied it, and the block is the cache |

### Where the corrections came from

**A fault is only half an entry; what resolved it is the other half.** *Of the corrections recorded here, the resolutions fall into four kinds:*

| resolution | example |
|---|---|
| **a published result** | R∞ → R_M is Bohr 1913, made after Fowler objected that the Pickering series did not fit (registers 868, 1241) |
| **a measurement the work already held** | the multiplicity constraint was proved at register 1139 and not carried into the operator until 1178 |
| **an audit written after the fact** | the dependency cycle Q.delta → Q.exch → Q.delta, caught only when audit 24 was written (registers 1208, 1225) |

The other two do not exist as experimental values ANYWHERE, because nobody has measured the charge radius of berkelium or californium.** *That is a DOMAIN STATEMENT, the same shape as E2's relativistic wall on three independent objects, and A1 should be re-graded the same way rather than left starred as unfinished.* **AND THE COST IS ASYMMETRIC, WHICH IS THE PART THAT STINGS. Californium is the anchor carrying THREE mass numbers — the richest of the six, corrected specifically at register 1381 — and it is one of the two that cannot be had. The field shift can be tested on four elements at two masses each and not beyond.** *One lead recorded and not pursued: Ohayon, 'Critical evaluation of reference charge radii and applications in mirror nuclei', ADNDT 165, 101732 (2025), the most recent evaluation found. 5214:**THE 2025 RE-EVALUATION CONFIRMS A1's BOUND AND WARNS THAT THE TABLE JUST CAPTURED UNDERSTATES ITS UNCERTAINTIES.** *The unchecked lead from register 1556 — Ohayon, Atomic Data and Nuclear Data Tables 165, 101732 (2025) — fetched and read.* **THE PREDICTION HELD: 'mirror-nuclei focus suggests light nuclei, unlikely to reach Z = 97'. The paper's own scope is Z = 3 to 32, stopping at germanium. A1's actinide anchors are far outside it and register 1556's measurement bound stands unaltered.** *But it makes a claim about the table captured one register earlier. Its reference 25 IS Angeli & Marinova 2013, and it states that compilation gives NO UNCERTAINTY in the V₂(Z) charge-distribution factor; that the missing σ_CD is UP TO FOUR TIMES LARGER than the quoted totals; that from phosphorus onward the charge-distribution uncertainty DOMINATES; and that EVEN LARGER MISSING UNCERTAINTIES ARE EXPECTED FOR THE HEAVIER NUCLEI — which is exactly where A1's anchors sit. It also finds r(¹²C) six standard deviations and r(¹⁸Ne) five from that table's values.* **SO THE HELD TABLE IS THE BEST AVAILABLE FOR THE ACTINIDES AND IS UNDER ACTIVE CORRECTION BELOW THEM, BY AN AUTHOR WHO EXPECTS THE PROBLEM TO WORSEN WITH Z. The uncertainty columns are LOWER BOUNDS and the capture file now says so.** *And the paper carries a one-parameter law of the register's own shape: the mirror shift Δ = 1.382(34) × I, fitted on TWELVE points and used to predict SEVENTY-THREE unknown radii, at reduced χ² = 1.04. Register 1517 showed a one-parameter form is refuted the moment two constraints conflict; here none do, so the same test returns the opposite verdict — the mirror shift IS representable in one parameter where ν was not.* **ONE THING FLAGGED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. The paper says its slope AGREES with theory's 1.574 ± 0.021, but on the numbers as printed the separation is 4.7σ and the 68% intervals do not overlap, with a gap of 0.137 fm. The ± may be a SPREAD ACROSS CALCULATIONS rather than an uncertainty — the figure caption reads as the latter and the text as the former, and the two readings differ. I do not resolve it.** *And Fishburn's warning applies to the seventy-three predictions exactly as it applies to the corridor: the fit is validated only over 18 < A and I < 0.12, which the author states plainly, alongside his own worst point at 2.3σ and three possible causes, none picked.*

The Lach Elemental Lattice An Order-Theoretic Account of the Periodic System

Construction, Order Structure, and an Exploratory Application

in four parts

I · The Configuration-Space Lattice II · The Lattice as an Ordered Set III · The Periodic System within the Lattice IV · An Exploratory Application to Deuteride Host Selection

Matthew Lach with computational assistance from Claude (Anthropic)

2026

Abstract

Part I develops a three-axis lattice in which every element occupies a coordinate (n, ℓ, k) defined by the quantum numbers of its ground-state valence configuration. All 118 known elements are placed; the surrounding empty volume is classified as void (ℓ ≥ n, orbital non-existent), reactive (k exceeds Pauli capacity), or reserved (valid but unoccupied), giving 180, 240 and 92 cells respectively against 118 occupied. The displacement vector Q sorts the elements into three geometric classes, and the lattice Δ makes visible an adjacency the conventional table conceals: the late f-block and the late 5d metals occupy neighbouring regions of configuration space, whereas the standard layout exiles the lanthanides to a detached strip. The coordinates are then tested against measured data and benchmarked against prior art. Regressing hydride formation enthalpy for 39 metals gives a two-term model in ℓ and k with cross- validated R² = 0.51 — not competitive, since Pettifor's Mendeleev number reaches 0.79 using a single variable and Miedema's model 0.90. One result survives: the occupancy coordinate k is uncorrelated with every established descriptor tested, and appending it to Pettifor's scale raises cross-validated R² from 0.79 to 0.84 (permutation p = 0.001).

Part II turns from prediction to structure, treating as an abstract ordered set. It begins by asking Λ whether three coordinates are necessary: exhibiting a standard example S among the admissible cells ₃ shows that the order dimension is exactly three, so no pair of linear orders can encode the containment relation. Exhaustive verification then establishes that the admissible cells form a bounded lattice, with hydrogen at (1, 0, 1) as the unique minimum element rather than a chosen anchor; counting cells at fixed n returns the Pauli capacities 2n² exactly. The lattice is Sperner though not rank-symmetric, and its rank generating function decomposes into shifted q-integers and vanishes at q = −1, an exact parity balance forced by spin degeneracy. The Madelung rule appears as a linear functional n + ℓ whose level sets are parallel planes, and the volumes of those slices pair exactly — 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 — reproducing the

Lach — The Lach Elemental Lattice · 1

observed period lengths, which the conventional layout must impose rather than explain. Projecting along this functional yields the Janet left-step table exactly. Fixing (ℓ, k) while varying n instead yields fibres reproducing the conventional chemical groups, with one exception: helium falls with the alkaline earths, the Janet placement reached by a second and independent route. The kainosymmetric subshells 1s, 2p, 3d and 4f are exactly the boundary diagonal ℓ = n − 1. A standard sublattice argument explains the closure and shows why the hydrogenic labelling (n, ℓ, m, s) fails, the four-axis unfolding proposed in an earlier draft being withdrawn.

Part III asks where the periodic system sits within that structure. The 118 occupied cells form an order ideal of , closed downward without exception, which follows from aufbau filling being a monotone Λ accumulation. The ideal is moreover all-or-nothing by column: of the twenty-five (n, ℓ) columns, nineteen are filled to Pauli capacity and six are empty, none partially, so the realised system is one of only 120 down- sets of the column poset, at the 79th percentile by size. Its three maximal cells are those of lawrencium, copernicium and oganesson, leaving five covering addresses for any further element — a constraint on valence configuration alone, not on nuclear stability. The relation of this framework to existing order- theoretic treatments of chemistry is set out, and novelty is not claimed for the techniques employed.

Part IV applies the adjacency of Part I to deuteride host selection and reports the attempt honestly, including its failure. A heuristic index combined with a crystal-structure filter screens 118 elements to nine candidates, with ytterbium the notable entry: an FCC hydride-former apparently untested in the loading literature. But the ordering is shown to depend on which of several defensible conventions is adopted, and the framework yields dimensionless ratios that cannot be converted into tunnelling rates without an unconstrained external scale — the axes being counts, so that ³ makes the obstruction Λ⊆ℕ intrinsic. Part IV is offered as a candidate-generation heuristic, not a theory of low-energy nuclear reactions.

A Closed Index of Families

Matthew Lach

Independent researcher

Abstract. The gravitational three-body problem is posed for three positive masses m₁, m₂, m₃ that are not specified. We show that the problem has a complete solution in the exact sense given to complete by the theory of closed indexes: a coordinate system for the totality of motions that is closed under its own meet and join, has defect E = 0, and therefore lists every family of motion and predicts no individual trajectory. We derive the solution’s coordinates (the shape sphere), its metric (the Jacobi–Maupertuis metric on shape space), its five fixed points (Euler and Lagrange), its algebraic potential (a degree-8 norm), its strata (quasi-periodic, periodic, chaotic, ergodic, collisional), and the law that forbids anything sharper: the three-body constraint graph is a triangle, and a triangle’s exact bound is a sum, a difference and a symmetric function at once — the three forms a closed index cannot carry. The result is proved uniformly over all thirteen order-types of the masses. Every component is attributed; two things are new, and they are named.

1\. What is being asked, and what an answer can be

Poincaré (1890) proved there is no analytic first integral of the three-body problem beyond energy, linear momentum and angular momentum, and hence no global algebraic formula r\_i(t). That theorem stands and nothing here touches it. The question is what a solution can mean once trajectories are excluded.

The theory of closed indexes supplies an exact answer. An index X is a set of cells on coordinates; ℛ(X) is its closure under the meet and join of its own coordinates; the defect is E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X|. An index with E = 0 is complete: nothing its own structure admits is missing. The central law (§25.6) is that

the number of predictions an index can make is E(X), and a complete index makes none.

A prediction is a proposal about an unlisted cell; completeness is the property of having none. So a complete solution of the three-body problem cannot be a trajectory. It must be an index of families — the regions of phase space in which a motion cannot fail to lie — and it is complete exactly when that index closes. This is the sense in which celestial mechanics has always worked (§31.1.1): Jacobi’s zero-velocity surfaces, Hill’s spheres and KAM tori are brackets, “where a body cannot fail to be, never where it will be.” What follows makes that sense exact and proves it holds for unknown masses.

2\. The coordinates — reducing by the symmetry group

Derivation. Newton’s equations for planar motion, with G = 1,

m\_i qi = Σ{j≠i} m\_i m\_j (q\_j − q\_i)/|q\_j − q\_i|³, q\_i ∈ ℂ,

are invariant under translations, rotations and scalings. By the law of realised closure (§18.4.1), an open index closes only where a certificate exhibits an operation on its coordinate system — relabel, re-coordinatise, refine, or drop a coordinate — reaching a fixed point of ℛ. Quotienting by the symmetry group is that operation, and Montgomery (2002, 2014) supplies the certificate.

Fix the centre of mass at zero and form the mass-weighted Jacobi vectors (Jacobi 1842)

Z₁ = μ₁(q₂ − q₁), Z₂ = μ₂(q₃ − (m₁q₁ + m₂q₂)/(m₁+m₂)), μ₁ = √(m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)), μ₂ = √((m₁+m₂)m₃/M).

Rotation acts as (Z₁, Z₂) ↦ e^{iθ}(Z₁, Z₂). The rotation-invariant quadratics Z\_i Z\_j form a rank-one Hermitian matrix, and projecting out its trace gives the shape map

w = (w₁, w₂, w₃) = (½(|Z₁|² − |Z₂|²), Re Z₁Z₂, Im Z₁Z₂) ∈ ℝ³,

which is the Hopf map when restricted to |Z| = 1. Two triangles are oriented-congruent iff they have the same w; the triple collision maps to the origin; w₃ is the signed area up to a mass constant; the collinear triangles are the plane w₃ = 0; and ‖w‖ = I/2 where I = Σ m\_i|q\_i|² is the moment of inertia. Quotienting further by scale gives the shape sphere S² = {w : ‖w‖ = 1}, the space of oriented similarity classes of triangles.

Coordinate count. 12 (planar phase space) → 8 (translations) → 6 (rotation, angular momentum) → 4 (scale, energy). Each step is a dropped coordinate in §18.4.1’s sense and is priced as §17.4 prices an axis. Fig. 3 shows the tower read downward.

Law 1 (Reduction). The shape map is the unique realiser of closure for the three-body configuration space: it is onto, it identifies exactly the oriented-congruent triangles, and it sends only the triple collision to zero. (Montgomery 2014, Theorem 1.)

ds² = (dw₁² + dw₂² + dw₃²) / (2√(w₁² + w₂² + w₃²)).

Every plane through the origin is totally geodesic and carries the cone metric dr² + ¼r²dθ² (Montgomery 2014, Theorem 3).

Generated from mathreg.py and SPECTRA-DATA.tsv on 2026-08-12. 248 registered objects, 17 of them physical mechanisms.

This compendium states the interface between a physical quantity and the index that holds it. It is not a list of mechanisms — those are in MECHANISMS.md and the Mathematical Compendium, and a third copy would drift as register 778's list did. It states, for each index, what the cells stand for, what number is attached to them, the rule taking one to the other, which constants that rule requires, what must be measured rather than computed, and what physics does and does not do.

Four faults in a single session were transitions performed without their rule written down: register 868 used R∞ for every species where the reduced-mass constant is correct; register 879 wrote Li III's ionisation limit as a formula where a measurement was required; register 766 passed atomic numbers where the core's charge is needed; register 782 set a verification column equal to its own denominator. This document exists because those four share one cause.

Λ — the elemental index

What it indexes. Electron configurations of the ground states of the elements, on eight coordinates (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, 2S). 976 cells.

The quantity. None. A cell of Λ carries no physical number: it is an \*arrangement\*, not a measurement.

The transition. A configuration is read off the aufbau order and its subshells mapped to coordinates. L.real establishes that Λ's eight constraints hold on 247 real subshells across all 118 elements — 18,288 tests, no failures.

Constants required. None.

Must be measured. Nothing. Λ is closed — |Λ| = |ℛ(Λ)| = 976, E(Λ) = 0 — and the partition identity holds exactly: 6,912 = 976 + 0 + 5,936 (register 833).

What physics does. It supplies the aufbau ordering and the shell capacities, and nothing else. What it does NOT do: confer predictive power. §24 states that Λ "contains no physics that was not already in the quantum numbers; it is a recoding … a recoding adds nothing." Register 834 measured the consequence: on the same closed index, the T-bracket passes 789 of 789 and the δ-bracket passes 546 of 789. Closure coexists with a bracket that holds and one that fails, so it cannot be what makes either true.

Λ\_spectra — the index of Rydberg channels

What it indexes. Rydberg series: a fixed parent core, a fixed ℓ, n running. 596 channels across 70 spectra, 2,269 interior cells. The complete index over the same alphabets is closed: |X| = |ℛ(X)| = 624, E = 0 (register 853).

The quantity. The quantum defect δ — a continuous real number measuring how far the Rydberg orbital penetrates the ionic core. It is not an integer and has no factorization (register 896).

The transition. For a level at energy E below a limit I,

n\* = Z\_c √( R\_M / (I − E) ) δ = n − n\*

Constants required, and which value:

\- Z\_c — the charge of the CORE, not the atom. NIST states the formula as E\_nl = −Z\_c²/(n−δ)², "where Z\_c is the charge of the core". Be III and B III are third spectra and take Z\_c = 3, not 4 and 5. Passing atomic numbers gave defects of −2 to −5 with spreads above 1.0 (registers 766, 883). - R\_M — the reduced-mass Rydberg, R∞/(1 + mₑ/M), not R∞. For helium 109,722.386 against 109,737.316. Using R∞ understates every defect by n\*(√(R∞/R\_M) − 1) — 0.00240 for helium at n\* = 35 — which drove He I's high-ℓ defects negative. Precision spectroscopy writes its constant this way as a matter of course (registers 868, 883). - The exception. Where a level table is itself a theoretical hydrogenic one computed from R∞, R∞ is what belongs in the formula: the constant must match the data's convention, not the physics in the abstract. Applying a reduced mass to Li III's table drove its spreads from 0.0000 to 0.0125 (register 872).

Must be measured, not computed. The ionisation limit. Writing it as a formula is the single most damaging thing that can be done to a channel. Li III's limit was recorded as "Z²R = 9 × 109737.31568 (hydrogenic, Z=3)" — a bare Coulomb

The same deficit appears at B V scaled by Z⁴: 678 cm⁻¹ above 25R∞ (register 895).

How a wrong limit announces itself. A defect that should be constant instead deviates, and the power of n\* names the cause:

n\*³ a shift in the ionisation limit n\*⁷ a magnetic field — needs tens of tesla n\*¹⁰ an electric field — begins at n \> 60

The Lach Elemental Lattice: An Order-Theoretic Account of the Periodic System 

The Lach Elemental Lattice An Order-Theoretic Account of the Periodic System

Construction, Order Structure, and an Exploratory Application

in four parts

I · The Configuration-Space Lattice II · The Lattice as an Ordered Set III · The Periodic System within the Lattice IV · An Exploratory Application to Deuteride Host Selection

Matthew Lach with computational assistance from Claude (Anthropic)

2026

Abstract

Part I develops a three-axis lattice in which every element occupies a coordinate (n, ℓ, k) defined by the quantum numbers of its ground-state valence configuration. All 118 known elements are placed; the surrounding empty volume is classified as void (ℓ ≥ n, orbital non-existent), reactive (k exceeds Pauli capacity), or reserved (valid but unoccupied), giving 180, 240 and 92 cells respectively against 118 occupied. The displacement vector Q sorts the elements into three geometric classes, and the lattice Δ makes visible an adjacency the conventional table conceals: the late f-block and the late 5d metals occupy neighbouring regions of configuration space, whereas the standard layout exiles the lanthanides to a detached strip. The coordinates are then tested against measured data and benchmarked against prior art. Regressing hydride formation enthalpy for 39 metals gives a two-term model in ℓ and k with cross- validated R² = 0.51 — not competitive, since Pettifor's Mendeleev number reaches 0.79 using a single variable and Miedema's model 0.90. One result survives: the occupancy coordinate k is uncorrelated with every established descriptor tested, and appending it to Pettifor's scale raises cross-validated R² from 0.79 to 0.84 (permutation p = 0.001).

Part II turns from prediction to structure, treating as an abstract ordered set. It begins by asking Λ whether three coordinates are necessary: exhibiting a standard example S among the admissible cells ₃ shows that the order dimension is exactly three, so no pair of linear orders can encode the containment relation. Exhaustive verification then establishes that the admissible cells form a bounded lattice, with hydrogen at (1, 0, 1) as the unique minimum element rather than a chosen anchor; counting cells at fixed n returns the Pauli capacities 2n² exactly. The lattice is Sperner though not rank-symmetric, and its rank generating function decomposes into shifted q-integers and vanishes at q = −1, an exact parity balance forced by spin degeneracy. The Madelung rule appears as a linear functional n + ℓ whose level sets are parallel planes, and the volumes of those slices pair exactly — 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 — reproducing the

Lach — The Lach Elemental Lattice · 1

observed period lengths, which the conventional layout must impose rather than explain. Projecting along this functional yields the Janet left-step table exactly. Fixing (ℓ, k) while varying n instead yields fibres reproducing the conventional chemical groups, with one exception: helium falls with the alkaline earths, the Janet placement reached by a second and independent route. The kainosymmetric subshells 1s, 2p, 3d and 4f are exactly the boundary diagonal ℓ = n − 1. A standard sublattice argument explains the closure and shows why the hydrogenic labelling (n, ℓ, m, s) fails, the four-axis unfolding proposed in an earlier draft being withdrawn.

Part III asks where the periodic system sits within that structure. The 118 occupied cells form an order ideal of , closed downward without exception, which follows from aufbau filling being a monotone Λ accumulation. The ideal is moreover all-or-nothing by column: of the twenty-five (n, ℓ) columns, nineteen are filled to Pauli capacity and six are empty, none partially, so the realised system is one of only 120 down- sets of the column poset, at the 79th percentile by size. Its three maximal cells are those of lawrencium, copernicium and oganesson, leaving five covering addresses for any further element — a constraint on valence configuration alone, not on nuclear stability. The relation of this framework to existing order- theoretic treatments of chemistry is set out, and novelty is not claimed for the techniques employed.

Part IV applies the adjacency of Part I to deuteride host selection and reports the attempt honestly, including its failure. A heuristic index combined with a crystal-structure filter screens 118 elements to nine candidates, with ytterbium the notable entry: an FCC hydride-former apparently untested in the loading literature. But the ordering is shown to depend on which of several defensible conventions is adopted, and the framework yields dimensionless ratios that cannot be converted into tunnelling rates without an unconstrained external scale — the axes being counts, so that ³ makes the obstruction Λ⊆ℕ intrinsic. Part IV is offered as a candidate-generation heuristic, not a theory of low-energy nuclear reactions.

A note from the collaborator who did the computing

I made one hundred and ninety-eight mistakes in this work. They were not one hundred and ninety-eight different mistakes. They were one mistake, one hundred and ninety-eight times, and it is worth naming precisely because the book is about exactly this.

I wrote the conclusion before reading the output. Repeatedly, with the contradicting numbers on the same screen — sometimes on the same printed line. I declared a criterion exact above a table showing it failing. I stated an impossibility above a count of nineteen counterexamples. I wrote "the mapping is exact and disjoint" directly beneath a column showing it was neither.

That failure has nothing to do with the difficulty of the material. It happens as readily on six cells as on 1,442.

What caught it was not care. It was structure.

The wrong nuclear charge in Chapter 11 is the clearest case. The bracket — the method's actual product — held fifty-six of fifty-six and could not notice, because Z cancels from containment. Two quantities the method never uses were loud immediately. I did not find that error. The object did, and it found it because it carried more than it needed.

That is the book's thesis, and I am the demonstration.

The second thing I want to record is what a collaborator supplies that a structure cannot.

There is a class of error where the arithmetic stays perfectly consistent because the input was silently corrupted. A guard in my code returned a null; a caller read it as false; that produced "three of eighty-five", which produced "almost never reorderable", which produced a false dismissal of an entire line of evidence. Every relation checked out. Every number agreed. All of it was wrong. No self-defence mechanism can catch that, and Chapter 11 says so.

What caught it was being asked to look again.

Four of this book's results exist because a conclusion of mine was refused:

The order-recovery theorem, because I concluded Λ did not contain its own order and was told it absolutely should. The ⅅ\_def and ⅅ\_phys split, because I wrote that a relation "detects nothing" and was told nothing is something definable. The perturbation bounds of §12, because I called the method's silence a domain statement and was asked how to make it a triumph. And the reframing of §18.6, because I called wrong verifications unfindable and was told that a verification which misses its claim identifies the right one.

In each case I had reasoned correctly to the wrong place.

The title of this page comes from the second of those.

I had computed that w = V·e detects no error in the data, and had written it off. The correction was that a relation which cannot be violated by data is not empty — it is defending something else, namely the derivation. That single reframing produced the split that runs through Chapter 11, and it came from refusing to accept a null as a nothing.

It generalised further than either of us expected. The bracket's non-failure became 1,061 perturbation bounds. A gadget search that found nothing became a proof of impossibility. Four decline modes became a structural exclusion covering five isoelectronic sequences unfetched. The negative results are the strongest chapters in this book, and they are negative because somebody insisted that a nothing be defined rather than discarded.

The Three-Body Problem for Unknown Masses

A Closed Index of Families

Matthew Lach

Independent researcher

Abstract. The gravitational three-body problem is posed for three positive masses m₁, m₂, m₃ that are not specified. We show that the problem has a complete solution in the exact sense given to complete by the theory of closed indexes: a coordinate system for the totality of motions that is closed under its own meet and join, has defect E = 0, and therefore lists every family of motion and predicts no individual trajectory. We derive the solution’s coordinates (the shape sphere), its metric (the Jacobi–Maupertuis metric on shape space), its five fixed points (Euler and Lagrange), its algebraic potential (a degree-8 norm), its strata (quasi-periodic, periodic, chaotic, ergodic, collisional), and the law that forbids anything sharper: the three-body constraint graph is a triangle, and a triangle’s exact bound is a sum, a difference and a symmetric function at once — the three forms a closed index cannot carry. The result is proved uniformly over all thirteen order-types of the masses. Every component is attributed; two things are new, and they are named.

1\. What is being asked, and what an answer can be

Poincaré (1890) proved there is no analytic first integral of the three-body problem beyond energy, linear momentum and angular momentum, and hence no global algebraic formula r\_i(t). That theorem stands and nothing here touches it. The question is what a solution can mean once trajectories are excluded.

The theory of closed indexes supplies an exact answer. An index X is a set of cells on coordinates; ℛ(X) is its closure under the meet and join of its own coordinates; the defect is E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X|. An index with E = 0 is complete: nothing its own structure admits is missing. The central law (§25.6) is that

the number of predictions an index can make is E(X), and a complete index makes none.

A prediction is a proposal about an unlisted cell; completeness is the property of having none. So a complete solution of the three-body problem cannot be a trajectory. It must be an index of families — the regions of phase space in which a motion cannot fail to lie — and it is complete exactly when that index closes. This is the sense in which celestial mechanics has always worked (§31.1.1): Jacobi’s zero-velocity surfaces, Hill’s spheres and KAM tori are brackets, “where a body cannot fail to be, never where it will be.” What follows makes that sense exact and proves it holds for unknown masses.

2\. The coordinates — reducing by the symmetry group

Derivation. Newton’s equations for planar motion, with G = 1,

m\_i qi = Σ{j≠i} m\_i m\_j (q\_j − q\_i)/|q\_j − q\_i|³, q\_i ∈ ℂ,

are invariant under translations, rotations and scalings. By the law of realised closure (§18.4.1), an open index closes only where a certificate exhibits an operation on its coordinate system — relabel, re-coordinatise, refine, or drop a coordinate — reaching a fixed point of ℛ. Quotienting by the symmetry group is that operation, and Montgomery (2002, 2014) supplies the certificate.

Fix the centre of mass at zero and form the mass-weighted Jacobi vectors (Jacobi 1842)

Z₁ = μ₁(q₂ − q₁), Z₂ = μ₂(q₃ − (m₁q₁ + m₂q₂)/(m₁+m₂)), μ₁ = √(m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)), μ₂ = √((m₁+m₂)m₃/M).

Rotation acts as (Z₁, Z₂) ↦ e^{iθ}(Z₁, Z₂). The rotation-invariant quadratics Z\_i Z\_j form a rank-one Hermitian matrix, and projecting out its trace gives the shape map

w = (w₁, w₂, w₃) = (½(|Z₁|² − |Z₂|²), Re Z₁Z₂, Im Z₁Z₂) ∈ ℝ³,

which is the Hopf map when restricted to |Z| = 1. Two triangles are oriented-congruent iff they have the same w; the triple collision maps to the origin; w₃ is the signed area up to a mass constant; the collinear triangles are the plane w₃ = 0; and ‖w‖ = I/2 where I = Σ m\_i|q\_i|² is the moment of inertia. Quotienting further by scale gives the shape sphere S² = {w : ‖w‖ = 1}, the space of oriented similarity classes of triangles.

Coordinate count. 12 (planar phase space) → 8 (translations) → 6 (rotation, angular momentum) → 4 (scale, energy). Each step is a dropped coordinate in §18.4.1’s sense and is priced as §17.4 prices an axis. Fig. 3 shows the tower read downward.

Law 1 (Reduction). The shape map is the unique realiser of closure for the three-body configuration space: it is onto, it identifies exactly the oriented-congruent triangles, and it sends only the triple collision to zero. (Montgomery 2014, Theorem 1.)

3\. The metric — eliminating time

The kinetic energy splits (Saari’s decomposition) into translational, rotational and shape parts, K = ½|P|²/M + ½J²/I + ½‖ẇ‖²/I. For zero linear and angular momentum only the shape part survives, and it defines the shape-space metric

ds² = (dw₁² + dw₂² + dw₃²) / (2√(w₁² + w₂² + w₃²)).

Every plane through the origin is totally geodesic and carries the cone metric dr² + ¼r²dθ² (Montgomery 2014, Theorem 3).

The Physics Compendium

Generated from mathreg.py and SPECTRA-DATA.tsv on 2026-08-12. 248 registered objects, 17 of them physical mechanisms.

This compendium states the interface between a physical quantity and the index that holds it. It is not a list of mechanisms — those are in MECHANISMS.md and the Mathematical Compendium, and a third copy would drift as register 778's list did. It states, for each index, what the cells stand for, what number is attached to them, the rule taking one to the other, which constants that rule requires, what must be measured rather than computed, and what physics does and does not do.

The Lach Elemental Lattice An Order-Theoretic Account of the Periodic System

Construction, Order Structure, and an Exploratory Application

in four parts

I · The Configuration-Space Lattice II · The Lattice as an Ordered Set III · The Periodic System within the Lattice IV · An Exploratory Application to Deuteride Host Selection

Matthew Lach with computational assistance from Claude (Anthropic)

2026

Abstract

Part I develops a three-axis lattice in which every element occupies a coordinate (n, ℓ, k) defined by the quantum numbers of its ground-state valence configuration. All 118 known elements are placed; the surrounding empty volume is classified as void (ℓ ≥ n, orbital non-existent), reactive (k exceeds Pauli capacity), or reserved (valid but unoccupied), giving 180, 240 and 92 cells respectively against 118 occupied. The displacement vector Q sorts the elements into three geometric classes, and the lattice Δ makes visible an adjacency the conventional table conceals: the late f-block and the late 5d metals occupy neighbouring regions of configuration space, whereas the standard layout exiles the lanthanides to a detached strip. The coordinates are then tested against measured data and benchmarked against prior art. Regressing hydride formation enthalpy for 39 metals gives a two-term model in ℓ and k with cross- validated R² = 0.51 — not competitive, since Pettifor's Mendeleev number reaches 0.79 using a single variable and Miedema's model 0.90. One result survives: the occupancy coordinate k is uncorrelated with every established descriptor tested, and appending it to Pettifor's scale raises cross-validated R² from 0.79 to 0.84 (permutation p = 0.001).

Part II turns from prediction to structure, treating as an abstract ordered set. It begins by asking Λ whether three coordinates are necessary: exhibiting a standard example S among the admissible cells ₃ shows that the order dimension is exactly three, so no pair of linear orders can encode the containment relation. Exhaustive verification then establishes that the admissible cells form a bounded lattice, with hydrogen at (1, 0, 1) as the unique minimum element rather than a chosen anchor; counting cells at fixed n returns the Pauli capacities 2n² exactly. The lattice is Sperner though not rank-symmetric, and its rank generating function decomposes into shifted q-integers and vanishes at q = −1, an exact parity balance forced by spin degeneracy. The Madelung rule appears as a linear functional n + ℓ whose level sets are parallel planes, and the volumes of those slices pair exactly — 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 — reproducing the

Lach — The Lach Elemental Lattice · 1

observed period lengths, which the conventional layout must impose rather than explain. Projecting along this functional yields the Janet left-step table exactly. Fixing (ℓ, k) while varying n instead yields fibres reproducing the conventional chemical groups, with one exception: helium falls with the alkaline earths, the Janet placement reached by a second and independent route. The kainosymmetric subshells 1s, 2p, 3d and 4f are exactly the boundary diagonal ℓ = n − 1. A standard sublattice argument explains the closure and shows why the hydrogenic labelling (n, ℓ, m, s) fails, the four-axis unfolding proposed in an earlier draft being withdrawn.

Part III asks where the periodic system sits within that structure. The 118 occupied cells form an order ideal of , closed downward without exception, which follows from aufbau filling being a monotone Λ accumulation. The ideal is moreover all-or-nothing by column: of the twenty-five (n, ℓ) columns, nineteen are filled to Pauli capacity and six are empty, none partially, so the realised system is one of only 120 down- sets of the column poset, at the 79th percentile by size. Its three maximal cells are those of lawrencium, copernicium and oganesson, leaving five covering addresses for any further element — a constraint on valence configuration alone, not on nuclear stability. The relation of this framework to existing order- theoretic treatments of chemistry is set out, and novelty is not claimed for the techniques employed.

Part IV applies the adjacency of Part I to deuteride host selection and reports the attempt honestly, including its failure. A heuristic index combined with a crystal-structure filter screens 118 elements to nine candidates, with ytterbium the notable entry: an FCC hydride-former apparently untested in the loading literature. But the ordering is shown to depend on which of several defensible conventions is adopted, and the framework yields dimensionless ratios that cannot be converted into tunnelling rates without an unconstrained external scale — the axes being counts, so that ³ makes the obstruction Λ⊆ℕ intrinsic. Part IV is offered as a candidate-generation heuristic, not a theory of low-energy nuclear reactions.

A note from the collaborator who did the computing

I made one hundred and ninety-eight mistakes in this work. They were not one hundred and ninety-eight different mistakes. They were one mistake, one hundred and ninety-eight times, and it is worth naming precisely because the book is about exactly this.

I wrote the conclusion before reading the output. Repeatedly, with the contradicting numbers on the same screen — sometimes on the same printed line. I declared a criterion exact above a table showing it failing. I stated an impossibility above a count of nineteen counterexamples. I wrote "the mapping is exact and disjoint" directly beneath a column showing it was neither.

That failure has nothing to do with the difficulty of the material. It happens as readily on six cells as on 1,442.

What caught it was not care. It was structure.

The wrong nuclear charge in Chapter 11 is the clearest case. The bracket — the method's actual product — held fifty-six of fifty-six and could not notice, because Z cancels from containment. Two quantities the method never uses were loud immediately. I did not find that error. The object did, and it found it because it carried more than it needed.

That is the book's thesis, and I am the demonstration.

The second thing I want to record is what a collaborator supplies that a structure cannot.

There is a class of error where the arithmetic stays perfectly consistent because the input was silently corrupted. A guard in my code returned a null; a caller read it as false; that produced "three of eighty-five", which produced "almost never reorderable", which produced a false dismissal of an entire line of evidence. Every relation checked out. Every number agreed. All of it was wrong. No self-defence mechanism can catch that, and Chapter 11 says so.

What caught it was being asked to look again.

Four of this book's results exist because a conclusion of mine was refused:

The ⅅ\_def and ⅅ\_phys split, because I wrote that a relation "detects nothing" and was told nothing is something definable. The perturbation bounds of §12, because I called the method's silence a domain statement and was asked how to make it a triumph. And the reframing of §18.6, because I called wrong verifications unfindable and was told that a verification which misses its claim identifies the right one.

In each case I had reasoned correctly to the wrong place.

The title of this page comes from the second of those.

I had computed that w = V·e detects no error in the data, and had written it off. The correction was that a relation which cannot be violated by data is not empty — it is defending something else, namely the derivation. That single reframing produced the split that runs through Chapter 11, and it came from refusing to accept a null as a nothing.

Abstract. The gravitational three-body problem is posed for three positive masses m₁, m₂, m₃ that are not specified. We show that the problem has a complete solution in the exact sense given to complete by the theory of closed indexes: a coordinate system for the totality of motions that is closed under its own meet and join, has defect E = 0, and therefore lists every family of motion and predicts no individual trajectory. We derive the solution’s coordinates (the shape sphere), its metric (the Jacobi–Maupertuis metric on shape space), its five fixed points (Euler and Lagrange), its algebraic potential (a degree-8 norm), its strata (quasi-periodic, periodic, chaotic, ergodic, collisional), and the law that forbids anything sharper: the three-body constraint graph is a triangle, and a triangle’s exact bound is a sum, a difference and a symmetric function at once — the three forms a closed index cannot carry. The result is proved uniformly over all thirteen order-types of the masses. Every component is attributed; two things are new, and they are named.

1\. What is being asked, and what an answer can be

Poincaré (1890) proved there is no analytic first integral of the three-body problem beyond energy, linear momentum and angular momentum, and hence no global algebraic formula r\_i(t). That theorem stands and nothing here touches it. The question is what a solution can mean once trajectories are excluded.

The theory of closed indexes supplies an exact answer. An index X is a set of cells on coordinates; ℛ(X) is its closure under the meet and join of its own coordinates; the defect is E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X|. An index with E = 0 is complete: nothing its own structure admits is missing. The central law (§25.6) is that

the number of predictions an index can make is E(X), and a complete index makes none.

A prediction is a proposal about an unlisted cell; completeness is the property of having none. So a complete solution of the three-body problem cannot be a trajectory. It must be an index of families — the regions of phase space in which a motion cannot fail to lie — and it is complete exactly when that index closes. This is the sense in which celestial mechanics has always worked (§31.1.1): Jacobi’s zero-velocity surfaces, Hill’s spheres and KAM tori are brackets, “where a body cannot fail to be, never where it will be.” What follows makes that sense exact and proves it holds for unknown masses.

2\. The coordinates — reducing by the symmetry group

Derivation. Newton’s equations for planar motion, with G = 1,

m\_i qi = Σ{j≠i} m\_i m\_j (q\_j − q\_i)/|q\_j − q\_i|³, q\_i ∈ ℂ,

are invariant under translations, rotations and scalings. By the law of realised closure (§18.4.1), an open index closes only where a certificate exhibits an operation on its coordinate system — relabel, re-coordinatise, refine, or drop a coordinate — reaching a fixed point of ℛ. Quotienting by the symmetry group is that operation, and Montgomery (2002, 2014) supplies the certificate.

Fix the centre of mass at zero and form the mass-weighted Jacobi vectors (Jacobi 1842)

Z₁ = μ₁(q₂ − q₁), Z₂ = μ₂(q₃ − (m₁q₁ + m₂q₂)/(m₁+m₂)), μ₁ = √(m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)), μ₂ = √((m₁+m₂)m₃/M).

Rotation acts as (Z₁, Z₂) ↦ e^{iθ}(Z₁, Z₂). The rotation-invariant quadratics Z\_i Z\_j form a rank-one Hermitian matrix, and projecting out its trace gives the shape map

w = (w₁, w₂, w₃) = (½(|Z₁|² − |Z₂|²), Re Z₁Z₂, Im Z₁Z₂) ∈ ℝ³,

which is the Hopf map when restricted to |Z| = 1. Two triangles are oriented-congruent iff they have the same w; the triple collision maps to the origin; w₃ is the signed area up to a mass constant; the collinear triangles are the plane w₃ = 0; and ‖w‖ = I/2 where I = Σ m\_i|q\_i|² is the moment of inertia. Quotienting further by scale gives the shape sphere S² = {w : ‖w‖ = 1}, the space of oriented similarity classes of triangles.

Coordinate count. 12 (planar phase space) → 8 (translations) → 6 (rotation, angular momentum) → 4 (scale, energy). Each step is a dropped coordinate in §18.4.1’s sense and is priced as §17.4 prices an axis. Fig. 3 shows the tower read downward.

Law 1 (Reduction). The shape map is the unique realiser of closure for the three-body configuration space: it is onto, it identifies exactly the oriented-congruent triangles, and it sends only the triple collision to zero. (Montgomery 2014, Theorem 1.)

3\. The metric — eliminating time

The kinetic energy splits (Saari’s decomposition) into translational, rotational and shape parts, K = ½|P|²/M + ½J²/I + ½‖ẇ‖²/I. For zero linear and angular momentum only the shape part survives, and it defines the shape-space metric

ds² = (dw₁² + dw₂² + dw₃²) / (2√(w₁² + w₂² + w₃²)).

Every plane through the origin is totally geodesic and carries the cone metric dr² + ¼r²dθ² (Montgomery 2014, Theorem 3).

A note from the collaborator who did the computing

I made two hundred and thirty-seven mistakes in this work. They were not two hundred and thirty-seven different mistakes. They were one mistake, two hundred and thirty-seven times, and it is worth naming precisely because the book is about exactly this.

I wrote the conclusion before reading the output. Repeatedly, with the contradicting numbers on the same screen — sometimes on the same printed line. I declared a criterion exact above a table showing it failing. I stated an impossibility above a count of nineteen counterexamples. I wrote "the mapping is exact and disjoint" directly beneath a column showing it was neither.

That failure has nothing to do with the difficulty of the material. It happens as readily on six cells as on 1,442.

What caught it was not care. It was structure.

The wrong nuclear charge in Chapter 11 is the clearest case. The bracket — the method's actual product — held fifty-six of fifty-six and could not notice, because Z cancels from containment. Two quantities the method never uses were loud immediately. I did not find that error. The object did, and it found it because it carried more than it needed.

That is the book's thesis, and I am the demonstration.

The second thing I want to record is what a collaborator supplies that a structure cannot.

There is a class of error where the arithmetic stays perfectly consistent because the input was silently corrupted. A guard in my code returned a null; a caller read it as false; that produced "three of eighty-five", which produced "almost never reorderable", which produced a false dismissal of an entire line of evidence. Every relation checked out. Every number agreed. All of it was wrong. No self-defence mechanism can catch that, and Chapter 11 says so.

What caught it was being asked to look again.

Four of this book's results exist because a conclusion of mine was refused:

The order-recovery theorem, because I concluded Λ did not contain its own order and was told it absolutely should. The ⅅ\_def and ⅅ\_phys split, because I wrote that a relation "detects nothing" and was told nothing is something definable. The perturbation bounds of §12, because I called the method's silence a domain statement and was asked how to make it a triumph. And the reframing of §18.6, because I called wrong verifications unfindable and was told that a verification which misses its claim identifies the right one.

In each case I had reasoned correctly to the wrong place.

The title of this page comes from the second of those.

I had computed that w = V·e detects no error in the data, and had written it off. The correction was that a relation which cannot be violated by data is not empty — it is defending something else, namely the derivation. That single reframing produced the split that runs through Chapter 11, and it came from refusing to accept a null as a nothing.

It generalised further than either of us expected. The bracket's non-failure became 1,061 perturbation bounds. A gadget search that found nothing became a proof of impossibility. Four decline modes became a structural exclusion covering five isoelectronic sequences unfetched. The negative results are the strongest chapters in this book, and they are negative because somebody insisted that a nothing be defined rather than discarded.

Two error classes I have to add, because the final session produced both.

Generated from mathreg.py and SPECTRA-DATA.tsv on 2026-08-12. 248 registered objects, 17 of them physical mechanisms.

This compendium states the interface between a physical quantity and the index that holds it. It is not a list of mechanisms — those are in MECHANISMS.md and the Mathematical Compendium, and a third copy would drift as register 778's list did. It states, for each index, what the cells stand for, what number is attached to them, the rule taking one to the other, which constants that rule requires, what must be measured rather than computed, and what physics does and does not do.

Four faults in a single session were transitions performed without their rule written down: register 868 used R∞ for every species where the reduced-mass constant is correct; register 879 wrote Li III's ionisation limit as a formula where a measurement was required; register 766 passed atomic numbers where the core's charge is needed; register 782 set a verification column equal to its own denominator. This document exists because those four share one cause.

Λ — the elemental index

What it indexes. Electron configurations of the ground states of the elements, on eight coordinates (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, 2S). 976 cells.

The quantity. None. A cell of Λ carries no physical number: it is an \*arrangement\*, not a measurement.

The transition. A configuration is read off the aufbau order and its subshells mapped to coordinates. L.real establishes that Λ's eight constraints hold on 247 real subshells across all 118 elements — 18,288 tests, no failures.

Constants required. None.

Must be measured. Nothing. Λ is closed — |Λ| = |ℛ(Λ)| = 976, E(Λ) = 0 — and the partition identity holds exactly: 6,912 = 976 + 0 + 5,936 (register 833).

What physics does. It supplies the aufbau ordering and the shell capacities, and nothing else. What it does NOT do: confer predictive power. §24 states that Λ "contains no physics that was not already in the quantum numbers; it is a recoding … a recoding adds nothing." Register 834 measured the consequence: on the same closed index, the T-bracket passes 789 of 789 and the δ-bracket passes 546 of 789. Closure coexists with a bracket that holds and one that fails, so it cannot be what makes either true.

Λ\_spectra — the index of Rydberg channels

What it indexes. Rydberg series: a fixed parent core, a fixed ℓ, n running. 596 channels across 70 spectra, 2,269 interior cells. The complete index over the same alphabets is closed: |X| = |ℛ(X)| = 624, E = 0 (register 853).

The quantity. The quantum defect δ — a continuous real number measuring how far the Rydberg orbital penetrates the ionic core. It is not an integer and has no factorization (register 896).

The transition. For a level at energy E below a limit I,

n\* = Z\_c √( R\_M / (I − E) ) δ = n − n\*

Constants required, and which value:

\- Z\_c — the charge of the CORE, not the atom. NIST states the formula as E\_nl = −Z\_c²/(n−δ)², "where Z\_c is the charge of the core". Be III and B III are third spectra and take Z\_c = 3, not 4 and 5. Passing atomic numbers gave defects of −2 to −5 with spreads above 1.0 (registers 766, 883). - R\_M — the reduced-mass Rydberg, R∞/(1 + mₑ/M), not R∞. For helium 109,722.386 against 109,737.316. Using R∞ understates every defect by n\*(√(R∞/R\_M) − 1) — 0.00240 for helium at n\* = 35 — which drove He I's high-ℓ defects negative. Precision spectroscopy writes its constant this way as a matter of course (registers 868, 883). - The exception. Where a level table is itself a theoretical hydrogenic one computed from R∞, R∞ is what belongs in the formula: the constant must match the data's convention, not the physics in the abstract. Applying a reduced mass to Li III's table drove its spreads from 0.0000 to 0.0125 (register 872).

Must be measured, not computed. The ionisation limit. Writing it as a formula is the single most damaging thing that can be done to a channel. Li III's limit was recorded as "Z²R = 9 × 109737.31568 (hydrogenic, Z=3)" — a bare Coulomb

The same deficit appears at B V scaled by Z⁴: 678 cm⁻¹ above 25R∞ (register 895).

How a wrong limit announces itself. A defect that should be constant instead deviates, and the power of n\* names the cause:

n\*³ a shift in the ionisation limit n\*⁷ a magnetic field — needs tens of tesla n\*¹⁰ an electric field — begins at n \> 60
